passage:
Last year I turned down the promotion to the Dubai office. Everyone at work thought I'd lost my mind. My cousin Shreya sent six messages with question marks.
I'm Seema. For most of my twenties, I made decisions by imagining the reactions first. Would my parents boast about it? Would my colleagues be impressed? I'd collect the “wow”s and feel good for a day.
This time, before telling anyone, I sat with a notebook and wrote what I actually value: being near my grandmother while she's still well, the Saturday reading class I run for kids, work that lets me sleep. Then I asked myself: would I be proud of this choice if nobody clapped?
Yes. Quietly, yes.
I still wanted people to understand. When Shreya's messages came, it stung. But it didn't shake me the way it once would have.

qa.a: Shreya sent six messages with question marks.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when Shreya's messages came?
qa.a: Seema felt stung but steady, because the choice was already checked against Seema's own values rather than others' reactions.

qa.q: What did Seema do before telling anyone, and why did it help?
qa.a: Seema wrote down personal values and asked whether the choice would feel right without applause, which loosened the grip of others' approval.

Mentor's note, fellowship programme, month 6.
Jahnavi has always checked in with me before every decision, often asking, “What would you do?” and watching my face for approval.
This month she was deciding whether to take her project to a small tribal school in Jharkhand instead of the high-profile city school the programme prefers. Her friend Dilnaz, also a fellow, told her the city school “looks better on a CV.”
This time she did something different. She came to our meeting with a page of her own reasons: the students' need, her language skills, what she wants to have learned by the end. She said, “I've decided. I'd be proud of this even if nobody noticed. I wanted you to know, not to check.”
She was visibly nervous saying it, but steady.
What I did next: I told her I respected the reasoning, and I stopped offering my view unless asked. We'll review the project together in month 9.

Saturday.
Posted the first episode of my Urdu poetry podcast today. Eleven listens. Pankaj's travel vlog got four thousand this week.
Old me would have spent all evening refreshing, feeling like a joke.
Instead I did what I promised myself last month. Before I checked anything, I wrote three lines: Why did I make this? Because my grandfather's poems deserve to be heard. Would I be proud of it if nobody clapped? Yes. Did I do it well? Mostly. The audio in the second half is rough.
Then I checked. Eleven.
It hurt a bit. I'd be lying if I said it didn't. I still want people to love it.
But the hurt had edges this time. It didn't swallow the whole evening. I made tea and started planning episode two.

In the village school at Rampur, the teacher gave Alka a sheet of long-division sums for the whole last hour. Hard ones. She worked through them all, tongue out, rubbing out, trying again.
When the bell rang, she walked home along the canal with her brother Farhan, feeling wrung out.
At home, Ammi had kept a tin of laddoos for the evening guests. “Don't touch these,” she said.
Alka touched them. She ate two, then a third.
When Farhan said, “You'll get caught,” she snapped, “Mind your own business!” and shoved him.
Later, after roti and a nap on the charpai, she felt awful. “Sorry, Farhan,” she mumbled. “I was so tired from those sums. I just couldn't stop myself.”
Farhan shrugged. “You were really grumpy.”

Jana had spent an hour at the kitchen table in Brno on her maths competition practice: fractions, then tricky word problems. When she finally closed the book, her head felt heavy.
Her little brother Bilal was eating crisps on the sofa. Usually Jana would have ignored him. Today she grabbed the bag. “Give me some.”
“Mum said no crisps before dinner!”
“You're eating them!”
They argued. Jana ate half the bag. When Bilal tried to take it back, she pushed his hand away hard.
Their mother came in. “What's going on?”
“I don't know,” Jana said, surprised at herself. “I'm just… tired. My brain's done.”
Mum looked at the maths book. “Hard session?”
Jana nodded. Mum handed her a glass of water. “Go outside for ten minutes. Then dinner.”

The olympiad training camp at the school ran from two to three: a full hour of geometry proofs. Jasleen, eleven, pushed through every one, even when her eyes blurred.
At three, the canteen opened. Jasleen had promised her mother no fried snacks this week. She bought two samosas.

Siddharth stared. “It was an accident.”
Jasleen sat on the steps and put her head in her hands. She knew she'd been rude. She also felt too tired to be sorry properly.
The camp teacher sat beside her. “Heavy hour, hmm? Brains get tired after proofs. Let's sit for five minutes.” After a while, Jasleen looked up and said, “Sorry, Siddharth.”

passage:
The psychology department seminar room smelled of old coffee. Uma's slide read: “Willpower as fuel: what the big replications found.”
She explained it plainly: early studies suggested self-control uses up a limited supply. But when many labs repeated the key tests together, the strong effect mostly didn't show up. Some research hinted that what people believe about tiredness might matter too.
Nilesh, at the back, yawned. “But I am depleted. I had two exams today.”
“You are tired,” Uma said. “That's real. I just don't think we know it's because a tank ran empty.”
He frowned, half annoyed. “So I'm imagining it?”
“No. Tiredness is real. Low motivation is real. The mechanism is what's uncertain.”
The professor nodded slowly. Uma sat down, heart thumping, a little unsure of herself but glad she'd said it carefully.

qa.q: What was written on Uma's slide?
qa.a: “Willpower as fuel: what the big replications found.”

qa.q: How did Uma feel after presenting?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with her heart thumping and a little unsure, but glad she had explained the uncertainty carefully.

qa.q: What made Uma's answer to Nilesh balanced?
qa.a: She agreed his tiredness was real while saying the fuel-tank explanation is uncertain, instead of dismissing him.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see the argument at first?
qa.a: Nilesh feels a bit annoyed and defensive, hearing it as if his tiredness were imaginary.

grounding: The seminar scene shows a psychology student explaining that large replications did not confirm strong depletion effects, while treating tiredness as real.

Subject: The willpower thing you told us about

Dear Shalini Ma'am,

Do you remember telling our Class 12 group that willpower is like a muscle that gets tired? I believed it completely. I used it as my excuse for everything.

This semester, in my research methods course, we read about how that idea was tested again by many labs working together. The big effect mostly didn't hold up. Some studies suggest that people who believe willpower runs out may give up sooner.

I felt a bit cheated at first. Then more curious. My tiredness after a long day is real. My low motivation is real. But the neat explanation isn't settled.

I'm not saying you were wrong to tell us. It was what the research said then. I just thought you'd like to know how the story changed.

Warm regards,
Rafiq

So you're asking why I stopped saying “I'm out of willpower,” Sarita. Okay, short version.
I'm Amandeep, second-year psych. Last month our professor showed us something. That famous idea, that self-control is like a tank that empties, came from lots of small studies. When dozens of labs ran the same test together, much more carefully, the big effect mostly wasn't there.
I was honestly shocked. I'd built my whole study routine around “saving” willpower.
There's also some work suggesting that if you believe you're running out, you might act like it.
Now, I'm not saying tiredness is fake. After a nine-hour day I'm wrecked. That's real. Low motivation is real. I just don't say it's “a tank” anymore. Nobody's sure what's going on underneath. I kind of like that honesty.

By seven in the evening, I've usually made about a hundred decisions. I'm Uma, I run scheduling at a hospital, and every hour is a string of “can you swap my shift?” and “which ward gets the extra nurse?”
That's why, every night, the gym bag I packed at 6 a.m. stays by the door. I tell myself I'll go. Then I open the food app and order biryani. Every night.
My flatmate Gopika asked if I was just tired. I said yes. Then I wondered. Maybe it's also that the gym is boring after a day like mine, and the sofa feels like the only thing I chose for myself.
Whatever it is, I've stopped arguing with 7 p.m. me. I moved the gym to 6:30 a.m., before the decisions start. And I cook dal on Sundays, so the evening choice is already made.

For years I blamed myself for being lazy. I'm Dhruv, I write software, and I used to leave the hardest code for the evening, after meetings, when I felt like I'd been through a washing machine. Of course it never got done.
Then I watched my colleague Nandini. She did her toughest work from 9 to 11, phone in a drawer, no meetings allowed. After lunch, she did emails and reviews. In the evening she didn't decide anything; her dinner was prepped on Sunday and her gym clothes were laid out the night before.
I admired it so much I copied it. Hardest task at 9. Easy stuff after lunch. Dinner planned.
Within a month I'd finished a module I'd been avoiding for weeks. I didn't become a better person. I just stopped fighting my own clock.

Harish has been one of our most improved analysts this quarter. I want to note what changed, because it was not a sudden burst of discipline.

Harish's reports have been on time for eight straight weeks.

At the Sonpur mela, the balloon seller was packing up. Simran Aunty, who ran the tea stall next door, called out to Arnab, “If you help me stack cups till the lights come on, I'll give you two balloons instead of one.”
Arnab, nine, shook his head. “One now, please.”
Aunty laughed. “Two is more!”
Arnab didn't smile. At last year's mela, a man had promised him a big-wheel ride for carrying water, then vanished. At school, prizes promised by the sir never came.
“One now,” he said again, quietly.

You asked how my marks went up this term, Anand. It's embarrassing, but okay.
I'm Ayesha. Last year, I'd sit down to revise, and my phone would buzz. “Your crops are ready!” from that farming game. I'd check “just for a second.” Forty minutes gone.

So now, before I revise, I mute all game notifications and put the phone in Ammi's room, on her cupboard. I can't hear it, I can't see it.
Honestly? The first few days were strange. I kept reaching for my pocket. But then I'd get through a whole chapter without once thinking about crops. My chemistry went from 58 to 74.

qa.a: Changing the environment removes the cue, so Ayesha doesn't have to fight temptation every minute.

Madhuri, you're sixteen and you say the game keeps pulling you from your books. Let me, your Noor Apa, tell you what I did at your age. It wasn't that long ago.

Mohit, our twenty-year-old trainee, has had a noticeable effect on the four-year-olds, especially Hemant, who used to grab snacks before others were served and cry if made to wait.

Thursday night.
Sachin is six and he used to scream if he had to wait even a minute. Since Ma started her night shifts, it's mostly me looking after him after college.
I've been trying two things. First, I only promise what I can actually do, and then I do it. If I say “one cartoon after homework,” he gets one cartoon after homework. No forgetting.
Second, when he has to wait, we sing. Today the pressure cooker needed three whistles before dinner. We sang “one whistle, two whistles” and clapped each one.
Tonight he waited for all three. He didn't cry. When I served the dal, he said, “You always do what you say, Mahi Didi.”
I had to turn around so he wouldn't see my eyes. I'm twenty and I'm tired. But this feels worth it.
— Mahima

qa.a: It needed three whistles.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when Sachin said “You always do what you say”?
qa.a: She felt deeply moved and a little tearful, turning away so he wouldn't see.

qa.q: What two things is Mahima doing to help Sachin wait?
qa.a: Keeping every small promise and singing during waits, which teaches him that waiting is reliable and bearable.

qa.a: Sachin seems calmer and trusting, since he knows his sister keeps her word.

grounding: The diary shows a young caregiver keeping small promises and using songs during waits, helping a child learn that waiting pays.

passage:
Subject: The plan actually worked

Dear Sarita Di,

You told me in the summer to stop saying “I'll study more” and make an if-then plan instead. I thought it sounded too simple. I was wrong.

My plan: If it's after dinner, then I open my maths book before I touch my phone. That's it. No “maybe,” no deciding.

The first week was hard. I'd finish dinner and my hand would reach for the phone. But then I'd remember the rule and open the book. After about ten days, it became automatic. I don't even think about it now.

My maths test last week: 78. Last term I got 54.

I think the trick is that I don't have to choose every night. The choice was already made.

Thank you.
Sumit

qa.q: What was Sumit's if-then plan?
qa.a: If it's after dinner, then Sumit opens the maths book before touching the phone.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel in the first week of the plan?
qa.a: Sumit felt tempted and it was hard, with a hand reaching for the phone, before the habit became automatic.

qa.q: Why did the if-then plan work for Sumit?
qa.a: A specific cue, after dinner, linked to a set action meant there was no nightly choice to make.

qa.q: How might Sarita Di feel reading this email?
qa.a: Sarita Di would likely feel happy and proud that the advice helped Sumit's marks go up.

grounding: The email shows a teenager using an if-then plan linking after dinner to opening the maths book, reducing reliance on in-the-moment choices.

Rekha, you keep asking how I got my science marks up. Okay, here's the whole secret, and it's going to sound stupid.
I'm Ishita. Every night, I used to finish dinner, pick up my phone “for five minutes,” and look up and it'd be eleven. Every night I'd promise tomorrow would be different.
Then our counsellor told us about if-then plans. Not “I'll study harder.” Something exact.
So I made mine: If I've just put my plate in the sink, then I open the science book on the table before the phone.
That's it. Plate in sink, book open.
Week one I had to repeat it in my head like a mantra. By week three I didn't even think. Plate, book. My phone sits on the shelf until I've done an hour.
My science went from a C to a B-plus. It's not magic. It's just one less decision.

qa.q: What did Ishita's if-then plan link together?
qa.a: Putting the plate in the sink and opening the science book before the phone.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel about the nightly promises before the plan?
qa.a: Ishita felt frustrated and let down each night, promising tomorrow would be different.

qa.q: Why does the specific cue work better than “I'll study harder”?
qa.a: It ties a clear action to a daily event, so Ishita doesn't need to decide in the moment.

grounding: The monologue shows a teenager using an if-then plan tied to a specific cue after dinner, reducing reliance on in-the-moment choices.
